questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Asia is the world's largest continent. Roughly what fraction of the world's population lives there?
questions.hint: More than half of all people on Earth live in Asia.
questions.explanation: Around 60% (3/5) of the world's population lives in Asia. China and India alone hold over 2.8 billion people.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — How is Asia being transformed?

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name of the world's highest mountain range, which stretches across northern India, Nepal and Bhutan?
questions.hint: Home to Mount Everest.
questions.explanation: The Himalayas are the world's highest mountain range, formed by the Indian plate colliding with the Eurasian plate. They include Mount Everest (8,849 m).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — How is Asia being transformed?

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the world's highest mountain, found in the Himalayas?
questions.hint: 8,849 m above sea level — on the Nepal/China border.
questions.explanation: Mount Everest is 8,849 m high, on the border of Nepal and China (Tibet). It is the world's tallest mountain above sea level.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — How is Asia being transformed?

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which two tectonic plates are colliding to form the Himalayas?
questions.hint: One is named after India.
questions.explanation: The Indian plate is crashing into the Eurasian plate, pushing up the Himalayas by a few millimetres a year. This is a continental-continental collision.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — tectonics

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the longest river in Asia, which flows through China?
questions.hint: Sometimes called the 'Long River' in Chinese — Chang Jiang.
questions.explanation: The Yangtze (Chang Jiang) is Asia's longest river at around 6,300 km. It flows from Tibet to the East China Sea at Shanghai.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — How is Asia being transformed?

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What sacred river flows through northern India and is a vital water source for hundreds of millions of people?
questions.hint: It flows through Varanasi and into Bangladesh.
questions.explanation: The Ganges (Ganga) is a major Asian river flowing across northern India into Bangladesh, where it joins the Brahmaputra to form the world's largest delta.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — How is Asia being transformed?

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these is the largest desert in Asia?
questions.hint: It straddles China and Mongolia.
questions.explanation: The Gobi Desert covers parts of northern China and southern Mongolia. The Sahara is in Africa; the Atacama is in South America; the Mojave is in North America.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — world deserts

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are countries in Asia?
questions.hint: Egypt is in Africa. Brazil is in South America.
questions.explanation: India, China, Japan and Indonesia are all Asian countries. Egypt is in North Africa; Brazil is in South America.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — locational knowledge

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name of the seasonal wind system that brings heavy rain to South Asia in summer?
questions.hint: Starts with M — comes from an Arabic word for 'season'.
questions.explanation: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings heavy summer rains to South Asia. India relies on it for around 70% of its annual rainfall.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: During which months does the WET (summer) monsoon usually affect India?
questions.hint: Indian summer — when it's hottest.
questions.explanation: The wet monsoon typically lasts from June to September. Winds blow in from the Indian Ocean, bringing heavy rain that farmers depend on.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Why does the WET monsoon bring rain from the OCEAN onto the LAND?
options: The land heats up faster than the sea, so warm air rises over land and sucks moist air in from the sea
The sea heats up faster than the land, sending warm air inland
Winds always blow from west to east at this latitude
The Earth tilts so rain falls south in summer
questions.answer: The land heats up faster than the sea, so warm air rises over land and sucks moist air in from the sea
questions.hint: In summer, the LAND gets hotter than the sea.
questions.explanation: In summer the land heats up faster than the sea. Hot air rises over land, creating low pressure that pulls moist sea air inland. The moist air rises, cools and releases heavy rain.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Why does the DRY (winter) monsoon blow from the LAND towards the SEA?
options: The land is hotter than the sea, pushing winds out to sea
The land cools faster than the sea in winter, so high pressure forms over land and dry winds blow seawards
questions.answer: The land cools faster than the sea in winter, so high pressure forms over land and dry winds blow seawards
questions.hint: Winter = land cools FASTER than sea.
questions.explanation: In winter the land cools faster than the sea. High pressure builds over land, pushing dry winds out towards the warmer ocean. This brings a long dry season to India.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are POSITIVE impacts of the monsoon?
options: Cools temperatures after the hot dry season
answer: Cools temperatures after the hot dry season
questions.hint: POSITIVES = farming, water and power. Negatives = floods and landslides.
questions.explanation: Monsoon rains feed crops, refill reservoirs, cool temperatures, and power hydroelectricity. Flooding and landslides are negative impacts when the rains are too heavy.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are NEGATIVE impacts of the monsoon?
options: Deadly flooding in cities like Mumbai
answer: Deadly flooding in cities like Mumbai
questions.hint: Heavy rain = floods, landslides, ruined crops, disease.
questions.explanation: Negative monsoon impacts include floods, landslides, ruined crops, cholera and typhoid outbreaks, and crop failure. Refilled reservoirs is a POSITIVE.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Roughly what percentage of India's annual rainfall comes from the summer monsoon?
questions.hint: More than half — most of India's rain falls in just 4 months.
questions.explanation: Around 70–80% of India's annual rainfall arrives during the June–September wet monsoon. A weak monsoon can devastate farming and food prices.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — climate of South Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Put these steps of the wet (summer) monsoon in order.
options: Moist air rises, cools and condenses over India
Land heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean
Low pressure forms over the hot land, sucking in moist sea air
answer: Land heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean
Low pressure forms over the hot land, sucking in moist sea air
Moist air rises, cools and condenses over India
questions.hint: Start with WHY the land heats up. End with the RAIN.
questions.explanation: The wet monsoon: land heats faster than sea → low pressure forms over land → moist sea air pulled in → air rises, cools, condenses → heavy rain.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these South Asian countries is most regularly hit by major monsoon flooding because it sits on a huge low-lying delta?
questions.hint: Two massive rivers (Ganges and Brahmaputra) meet in this country.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh sits on the world's largest delta where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet. Most of the country is less than 10 m above sea level — monsoon floods cover huge areas each year.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon and floods

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are PHYSICAL causes of severe flooding in Bangladesh?
options: Tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal
answer: Tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal
questions.hint: Physical = natural. Tower blocks and deforestation are human factors.
questions.explanation: Physical causes: monsoon rain, Himalayan snowmelt swelling rivers, low-lying delta, and cyclones whipping up storm surges from the Bay of Bengal. Deforestation and building are HUMAN causes.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon and floods

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are HUMAN causes that make flooding in Bangladesh worse?
options: Urban growth in Dhaka covering soil with concrete
Cyclones forming over the Bay of Bengal
answer: Urban growth in Dhaka covering soil with concrete
questions.hint: Human = stuff people are responsible for. Cyclones and mountains are physical.
questions.explanation: Human causes include deforestation (less soil to absorb rain), urban concrete (water runs off), climate change (rising seas), and poor embankment maintenance. Cyclones are physical.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Monsoon and floods

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are ways Bangladesh tries to MANAGE flooding?
options: Early warning systems by phone and radio
Floating schools and houses on stilts
answer: Early warning systems by phone and radio
Floating schools and houses on stilts
questions.hint: You can't stop the monsoon or ban rain — but you CAN warn, shelter and build smart.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh uses embankments, cyclone shelters, warning systems and adaptive housing (floating schools, stilt homes). Stopping rain or the monsoon isn't possible.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Floods

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name of the giant delta in Bangladesh and India formed by the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers?
questions.hint: Named after the more famous of the two rivers — the world's largest delta.
questions.explanation: The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta (often called the Ganges Delta or Bengal Delta) is the world's largest. It covers most of Bangladesh and parts of West Bengal in India.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — physical geography of South Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name for a large-scale ecosystem with a distinct climate, plants and animals (e.g. tropical rainforest, tundra)?
questions.hint: 5 letters — Bio + me.
questions.explanation: A biome is a large-scale ecosystem defined by climate, plants and animals. Major biomes include tropical rainforest, desert, tundra, savanna and mountain.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Mountain biome

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which biome is found in the highest parts of the Himalayas?
questions.hint: Cold, windy, treeless at the top — mountain.
questions.explanation: The Himalayas have a mountain (alpine) biome at high altitudes — cold, low oxygen, thin soils, short growing season, hardy plants and animals like yaks and snow leopards.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Mountain biome

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are FEATURES of the mountain (alpine) biome in the Himalayas?
options: Lush dense rainforest at the peaks
Hardy plants like alpine flowers and lichens
answer: Hardy plants like alpine flowers and lichens
questions.hint: Mountain biome is COLD, WINDY, DRY — not lush rainforest.
questions.explanation: Mountain biomes have thin air, strong winds, cold temperatures, short growing seasons and tough plants like alpines and lichens. Rainforest is in tropical lowlands, not at peaks.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Mountain biome

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: From bottom to top, put these zones of a Himalayan mountainside in the correct order.
options: Deciduous and tropical forest at the base
answer: Deciduous and tropical forest at the base
questions.hint: Bottom = warmest. Top = coldest. Trees disappear before snow takes over.
questions.explanation: Going up the Himalayas: tropical/deciduous forest → coniferous forest → alpine meadow above the tree line → permanent snow and ice. Temperature drops about 6°C per 1,000m.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — mountain ecosystems

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What name is given to the altitude above which trees can no longer grow?
questions.hint: Two words — pretty literal.
questions.explanation: The tree line is the altitude above which it's too cold for trees to grow. Above this, you only get alpine plants, lichens, snow and rock.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — mountain ecosystems

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these animals are adapted to live in the Himalayan mountain biome?
questions.hint: Polar bears are Arctic. Camels are desert.
questions.explanation: Snow leopards, yaks, Himalayan tahrs and red pandas are all adapted to cold mountain conditions with thick fur and strong lungs. Polar bears live in the Arctic; camels in deserts.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — mountain biome adaptations

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are HUMAN threats to the Himalayan mountain biome?
questions.hint: Human = things people do. Plate tectonics and Earth's rotation are natural.
questions.explanation: Threats include climate change, tourism waste, deforestation and poaching. Plate tectonics and Earth's rotation are natural and not 'threats' caused by humans.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — environmental change

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: In which country is the state of Karnataka?
questions.hint: Indian state — its capital is Bangalore (Bengaluru).
questions.explanation: Karnataka is a state in southern India. Its capital, Bengaluru (Bangalore), is India's main IT and tech hub.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Karnataka, famous for its IT and tech industries?
questions.hint: Two acceptable names — its older English name was 'Bangalore'.
questions.explanation: Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore) is the capital of Karnataka. It's known as India's 'Silicon Valley' because of its huge tech industry.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Bengaluru is sometimes nicknamed India's…
questions.hint: Named after the famous US tech region in California.
questions.explanation: Bengaluru is called India's Silicon Valley because of its concentration of IT companies, call centres, software firms and tech start-ups.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons Bengaluru became India's IT hub?
options: Lower wages than the USA or UK
It has the highest mountains in India
Cool climate makes long working hours easier
Strong universities like the Indian Institute of Science
answer: Lower wages than the USA or UK
Cool climate makes long working hours easier
Strong universities like the Indian Institute of Science
questions.hint: Bengaluru is on a plateau (cool-ish) — NOT in the mountains.
questions.explanation: Bengaluru's IT boom came from skilled English-speaking graduates, government tech parks, cheaper costs than Western firms, a relatively cool climate (it's on a 900m plateau) and elite universities. It's not in the highest mountains.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are POSITIVE impacts of the IT boom on Karnataka?
options: Growing inequality between rich and poor
Strain on housing and water supply
questions.hint: Positive = the good stuff. Inequality and water strain are challenges.
questions.explanation: The IT boom raised wages, created skilled jobs, generated tax revenue and funded better infrastructure. Rising inequality and pressure on water/housing are negative side effects.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are NEGATIVE impacts of Bengaluru's rapid growth?
questions.hint: Rapid growth = strain on the city's resources and people.
questions.explanation: Bengaluru's growth has caused congestion, water shortages, lake pollution, loss of parks/green space, and the spread of informal settlements where poorer migrants live.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Karnataka

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: India as a whole is best described as a…
options: Very poor country with no industry
questions.hint: Three letters — N_E_E.
questions.explanation: India is a Newly Emerging Economy (NEE) — its economy is growing fast, with industry, services and tech booming, but big inequality remains.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the capital city of China?
questions.hint: Two syllables, starts with B. Was once spelled 'Peking'.
questions.explanation: Beijing is the capital of China and home to about 22 million people. It hosted the 2008 and 2022 Olympic Games.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: China is the world's…
options: Most populated country (in 2024 was overtaken by India)
questions.answer: Most populated country (in 2024 was overtaken by India)
questions.hint: Billions of people — only India has more.
questions.explanation: China was the world's most populous country for decades — until India overtook it in 2023. Both have over 1.4 billion people.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: China has the world's…
questions.hint: It's second only to the USA by total GDP.
questions.explanation: China has the world's second-largest economy by total GDP, behind only the USA. It is the world's biggest exporter of manufactured goods.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What nickname is China sometimes given because it produces so many of the world's manufactured goods?
questions.hint: Where the world makes stuff — three words.
questions.explanation: China is nicknamed 'the world's factory' because it manufactures around a third of global goods, from phones and toys to steel and clothes.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are commonly manufactured in China for export around the world?
questions.hint: Champagne is a protected French product, not made in China.
questions.explanation: China makes huge amounts of electronics, clothing, toys, steel and solar panels for global markets. Champagne is by law produced only in the Champagne region of France.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the term for countries relying on each other for trade, resources and finance?
questions.hint: One word — 'inter' (between) + 'dependence' (relying on).
questions.explanation: Interdependence is when countries depend on each other — for trade, jobs, resources or finance. Globalisation has made the UK and China deeply interdependent.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these show how the UK is INTERDEPENDENT with China?
options: UK imports phones, clothes and toys made in China
Chinese tourists visit Manchester and London
Chinese students study at UK universities
Chinese investment in UK infrastructure (e.g. nuclear power)
The UK supplies all of China's food
China shares a land border with the UK
answer: UK imports phones, clothes and toys made in China
Chinese tourists visit Manchester and London
Chinese students study at UK universities
Chinese investment in UK infrastructure (e.g. nuclear power)
questions.hint: The UK and China don't share a land border, and the UK doesn't feed China!
questions.explanation: The UK and China are linked through imports, tourism, education and investment. They don't share a border, and the UK doesn't supply all China's food.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What name does China give its huge global trade and infrastructure project, launched in 2013, building roads, railways and ports across Asia, Africa and Europe?
questions.hint: Three words — sometimes abbreviated to BRI.
questions.explanation: The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is China's massive plan to build trade routes, ports, railways and roads across more than 100 countries, expanding Chinese influence globally.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — global economy

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are POSITIVE impacts of China's rapid economic growth?
options: Hundreds of millions lifted out of poverty
Huge investment in cities and transport
Becoming a global leader in solar and electric cars
answer: Hundreds of millions lifted out of poverty
Huge investment in cities and transport
Becoming a global leader in solar and electric cars
questions.hint: Positive = the good outcomes.
questions.explanation: China's growth has lifted ~800 million people out of extreme poverty, built world-class infrastructure, made it a leader in renewables, and raised wages. Pollution and farmland loss are downsides.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are NEGATIVE impacts of China's rapid growth?
options: Severe air pollution in big cities
Loss of farmland to factories and cities
More people lifted out of poverty
Greenhouse gas emissions (now the world's largest)
answer: Severe air pollution in big cities
Loss of farmland to factories and cities
Greenhouse gas emissions (now the world's largest)
questions.hint: Negative = environmental/health problems. Life expectancy has actually RISEN.
questions.explanation: Negative impacts include air pollution, water shortages, loss of farmland and being the world's biggest CO2 emitter. Life expectancy has actually risen, and poverty has fallen.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name of the huge dam on the Yangtze river — the largest hydroelectric dam in the world?
questions.hint: Three words — named after three river canyons.
questions.explanation: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze is the world's largest hydroelectric power station. It generates massive clean energy but displaced over a million people and flooded ancient sites.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Roughly how many people have been lifted out of extreme poverty in China since 1980?
questions.hint: Hundreds of millions — about the population of Europe.
questions.explanation: Around 800 million Chinese people have been lifted out of extreme poverty since 1980 — the biggest reduction in poverty in human history.
questions.source: World Bank data — China poverty reduction

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which Chinese city is the country's biggest port and a major financial centre?
questions.hint: It's on the mouth of the Yangtze, with iconic skyscrapers across the Huangpu River.
questions.explanation: Shanghai is China's biggest port and financial centre, with over 26 million people. Its Pudong skyline is one of the most recognisable in the world.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — Chinese cities

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these phrases best describes Asia's role in the world economy today?
questions.hint: Think factories, tech, exports, megacities.
questions.explanation: Asia is now a global economic powerhouse — China, India, Japan, South Korea and Southeast Asian economies together make up nearly half of world GDP.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Asia as a global economic region

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are major Asian economies?
questions.hint: Argentina is in South America.
questions.explanation: China, Japan, India, South Korea and Indonesia are all major Asian economies. Argentina is in South America.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — Asian economies

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What term describes how countries, businesses and people around the world are increasingly connected?
questions.hint: Comes from the word 'global' — one word.
questions.explanation: Globalisation is the increasing connection between countries through trade, technology, travel and culture. It is what made China the world's factory and Bengaluru a tech hub.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Asia as a global economic region

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the term for a huge company that operates in many countries (e.g. Apple, Samsung)?
questions.hint: Three letters — T_N_C.
questions.explanation: A Transnational Corporation (TNC) is a company that operates in multiple countries — like Apple, Samsung, Toyota or Tata. TNCs are key drivers of globalisation.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — globalisation

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Why do many TNCs choose to locate factories in Asia?
options: Lower wages than in Europe or the USA
Looser environmental laws in some places
The shortest distance to the Moon
answer: Lower wages than in Europe or the USA
Looser environmental laws in some places
questions.hint: Distance to the Moon is the same everywhere on Earth!
questions.explanation: TNCs choose Asia for lower wages, big skilled workforces, looser regulations, excellent ports/infrastructure and government incentives. Distance to the Moon is irrelevant.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Asia as a global economic region

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these is the BEST evidence that Asia is becoming a global economic region?
options: Asian countries lead in manufacturing, exports, tech and finance
Asia has the largest desert in the world
Asia is mostly farming and has no factories
questions.answer: Asian countries lead in manufacturing, exports, tech and finance
questions.hint: Economic = jobs, exports, money, trade.
questions.explanation: Asia leads in manufacturing (China), tech (India, South Korea), finance (Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo) and exports — the clearest sign it is a global economic region.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Asia as a global economic region

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the term for a country whose economy is growing fast but is not yet as wealthy as a HIC (e.g. India, Brazil, Indonesia)?
questions.hint: Three letters — N_E_E.
questions.explanation: Newly Emerging Economies (NEEs) are countries growing fast through industry and services — like India, China, Brazil, Mexico and Indonesia. Their wealth is rising but unevenly.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which Asian country was the first to industrialise rapidly after WW2, becoming an HIC?
questions.hint: Famous for Toyota, Sony, Nintendo and bullet trains.
questions.explanation: Japan was the first Asian country to fully industrialise, becoming a High-Income Country (HIC) by the 1970s — known for car-making (Toyota), electronics (Sony) and bullet trains.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — Asian development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are famous Asian transnational corporations (TNCs)?
questions.hint: Lego is Danish. Tesla is American.
questions.explanation: Samsung, Toyota, Tata and Huawei are major Asian TNCs. Lego is Danish; Tesla is American.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — TNCs in Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Put these stages of Asia's economic transformation in chronological order.
options: India's IT boom in Bengaluru (1990s onwards)
Japan rebuilds as a manufacturing power (1950s–70s)
South Korea and the 'Asian Tigers' rise (1970s–80s)
China opens up and becomes 'the world's factory' (1980s onwards)
answer: Japan rebuilds as a manufacturing power (1950s–70s)
South Korea and the 'Asian Tigers' rise (1970s–80s)
China opens up and becomes 'the world's factory' (1980s onwards)
India's IT boom in Bengaluru (1990s onwards)
questions.hint: Start with Japan after WW2. End with India in the 90s.
questions.explanation: Asia's rise: Japan (1950s–70s) → Asian Tigers like South Korea (1970s–80s) → China (1980s onwards) → India (1990s onwards). Each wave used lessons from the last.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — Asian development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the collective nickname for South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore, which industrialised rapidly from the 1960s?
questions.hint: Named after a fierce big cat — strong and fast.
questions.explanation: The 'Asian Tigers' — South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore — were the first wave of fast-growing Asian economies after Japan, industrialising rapidly from the 1960s.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — Asian development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What is the name of the high plateau in central Asia, often called the 'Roof of the World'?
questions.hint: Named after a Chinese region — part of China today.
questions.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau in the world, averaging 4,500 m. It is the source of major rivers including the Yangtze, Mekong, Indus and Ganges.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — physical Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these major rivers have their SOURCE in the Himalayas or Tibetan Plateau?
questions.hint: The Thames is in England. The Nile is in Africa.
questions.explanation: The Ganges, Yangtze, Brahmaputra and Indus all start in the Himalayas or Tibetan Plateau. The Thames is in southern England; the Nile flows north through Africa.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — physical Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which Indian region is famous for receiving some of the world's heaviest monsoon rainfall?
questions.hint: Up against the foothills of the Himalayas, near Bangladesh.
questions.explanation: Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, in north-east India, receive over 11,000 mm of rain a year. Moist monsoon air is forced up by the hills and dumps enormous rainfall.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — extreme weather

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which sector employs the largest share of Karnataka's rural population?
questions.hint: Cities = IT. RURAL = ?
questions.explanation: Even though Bengaluru is the IT capital, most of Karnataka's RURAL population works in agriculture — rice, coffee, sugarcane and silk are key crops.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — uneven development

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Roughly what share of China's population lives in urban areas today?
questions.hint: It has more than doubled since 1980, when it was about 20%.
questions.explanation: About 65% of Chinese people now live in urban areas, up from around 20% in 1980. This is the largest internal migration in human history.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — urbanisation in Asia

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these measures economic development by averaging out a country's total income across its population?
questions.hint: 'Per capita' means 'per person'.
questions.explanation: GDP per capita is total GDP divided by the population — a quick measure of average income. Richer countries have higher GDP per capita.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — development indicators

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What does HDI stand for — a measure of development combining income, education and life expectancy?
questions.hint: Three words — starts with 'Human'.
questions.explanation: HDI (Human Development Index) combines GDP per capita, schooling and life expectancy into a single score 0–1. It gives a fuller picture than money alone.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — development indicators

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Roughly what proportion of Bangladesh is flooded in a typical monsoon year?
questions.hint: Bangladesh floods every year — but not the whole country.
questions.explanation: Around 20–30% of Bangladesh is flooded in a typical monsoon. In extreme years (like 1998) it can be 60–70%.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — flood risk

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: By approximately how much does temperature drop for every 1,000 metres climbed up a mountain?
questions.hint: Roughly 6 — that's why mountain summits are freezing even in summer.
questions.explanation: Temperature drops roughly 6°C for every 1,000 m gained. That's why a peak 5,000 m above a warm valley is bitterly cold.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — climate and altitude

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: What word describes plants and animals that have changed over time to survive in a particular environment?
questions.hint: Verb starting with A — like a TV show being changed for a new audience.
questions.explanation: Adapted species have features suited to their environment — yaks have thick fur, snow leopards have wide paws and big lungs, alpine plants stay small to escape wind.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 Geography — ecosystems

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these is one of China's MOST important exports?
questions.hint: China is 'the world's factory'.
questions.explanation: Manufactured goods — electronics, clothing, machinery, toys — are China's main exports. It is the world's largest exporting country.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — China

questions.subject: geography
questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons Asia has become so important to the global economy?
options: Huge populations providing both workers and consumers
Government-led economic planning in many countries
Strategic shipping routes (Strait of Malacca, South China Sea)
answer: Huge populations providing both workers and consumers
Government-led economic planning in many countries
Strategic shipping routes (Strait of Malacca, South China Sea)
questions.hint: Distance to the Moon is silly — ignore it.
questions.explanation: Asia's huge populations, industrial growth, investment in education and tech, strong state planning and strategic shipping routes have made it central to the global economy.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Geography KM, Summer — Asia as a global economic region
